column12: THE AHA FIGURE IN THE PREVALENCE ROW ABOVE CANNOT SUPPLY THIS AND WAS DELIBERATELY NOT USED. Martin SS, Aday AW, Allen NB et al., '2025 Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics', Circulation 2025;151(8):e41-e660, PMC12256702, Chapter 25 Incidence carries one rate: 'In the GBD Study 2019, the age-standardized incidence rate of PAD in the United States was 193.5 per 100 000 (95% UI, 173.7-215.6 per 100 000).' It is age-standardized, so multiplying it by a crude population is invalid, and the GBD paper behind it (Lancet Glob Health 2023;11:e1553-e1565, PMC10522777) models PAD only from age 40 while labelling its rates 'per 100 000 population' without saying which denominator. No absolute count of annual new US PAD cases exists in a free source; the AHA chapter and the GBD free text were both searched. Framingham was rejected too (Murabito JM et al., Am J Epidemiol 2005;162(5):430-437, PMID 16076834, '282 per 100,000 person-years ... to 225 per 100,000 person-years in the 1990s') because its endpoint is intermittent claudication rather than PAD and its data end in 1999, so using it would have swapped the case definition underneath an ABI-based prevalence. CROSS-CHECK: 734,843 a year into 12,400,000 prevalent implies 16.9 years in the pool, which is reasonable for disease first found at 65 to 70 and is the main reason to believe the rate and the prevalence describe the same population. ERRS LOW on two counts - ARIC's cohort was 45-64 and the rate is applied to everyone 45 and over, where incidence is higher; and the 12,400,000 subtracted is an aged-40-and-over count taken off a 45-and-over population. The alternative published ARIC rate, 6.2 per 1,000 person-years (Lutsey PL et al., Atherosclerosis 2017, PMC5369771), would give 813,576; Ogilvie's 5.6 is taken for the larger sample and longer follow-up.
